Block volume testing – Red Hat Enterprise Linux 9.2

  • This section examines the testing results for a RHEL 9.2 host configured as a PowerFlex CO node using PowerFlex storage.

    Testing observations – Red Hat Enterprise Linux using the 25GBbps Ethernet Adapter

    We tested with the bare-metal environment described in the System architecture section using four 25GbE Ethernet adapters. The fio tester was installed during the initial setup of the node.

    In the PowerFlex Manager UI we created three volumes of 320GB in size and presented them to four Red Hat hosts.

    The environment was then configured using the fio tool guidance. We issued the fio command from a console to run a 20% random write test. The configuration of the fio command is detailed in Appendix B – fio configuration for all test states.

    Testing observations – Red Hat Enterprise Linux Volumes using the 100GBbps Ethernet Adapter

    Following completion of the 25GbE Ethernet adapter testing, the environment was shut down and reconfigured with the 100GbE Ethernet adapters. This included the four PowerFlex SO nodes and the four Red Hat Enterprise Linux CO nodes.

    Using the reconfigured Red Hat Enterprise Linux environment described in the System architecture section with two 100GbE Ethernet adapters, fio was installed during the initial setup of the node. In the PowerFlex Manager UI we created 3 volumes of 320GB in size and presented them to the Red Hat host.

    The environment was then configured using the fio tool guidance. We then used the same fio commands from the previous section to obtain results for the 100GbE Ethernet adapter.

    Evaluation of results for Red Hat Enterprise Linux Volumes

    We have compiled the results in the following charts to show the comparison of the 25GbE and 100GbE Ethernet adapter. The following charts compare the throughput results of four 25GbE Ethernet adapters, two 100GbE Ethernet adapters, and four 100GbE Ethernet adapters.

    Figure 26.    RHEL 9.2 – Read Throughput Comparison – Four 25GbE vs. Two 100GbE vs. Four 100GbE Ethernet adapters

    Figure 27.    RHEL 9.2 – Write Throughput Comparison – Four 25GbE vs. Two 100GbE vs. Four 100GbE Ethernet adapters

    The test results show that two 100GbE Ethernet adapters provide an 89% improvement in 256k read throughput, and an 82% improvement in 1M read throughput compared to four 25Gbs Ethernet adapters. The improvement in writes is even greater with a 93% improvement in 256k write throughput and an 87% improvement in 1M write throughput. The two 100GbE Ethernet adapters are within 10% of the theoretical line rate of two 100GbE Ethernet adapters.

    This shows an increase in storage performance and means that it is more beneficial for a RHEL environment to use 100GbE Ethernet adapters when using PowerFlex for the underlying storage. This benefit can be seen across the different test scenarios performed.

    This also indicates that the optimal network configuration for a RHEL environment using PowerFlex as the underlying storage platform is to leverage 100GbE Ethernet adapters for optimal storage throughput as compared to 25GbE Ethernet adapters.

    Evaluation of results for SUSE Enterprise Linux Volumes

    We compiled the results in the following charts to show the comparison of the 25GbE and 100GbE Ethernet adapters:

    Figure 38.    SLES 15.4 – Read Throughput Comparison – Four 25GbE vs. Two 100GbE vs. Four 100GbE Ethernet adapters

    Figure 39.    SLES 15.4 – Write Throughput Comparison – Four 25GbE vs. Two 100GbE vs. Four 100GbE Ethernet adapters

    The test results show that two 100GbE Ethernet adapters provide a 94% improvement in 256k read throughput and an 88% improvement in 1M read throughput, compared to four 25Gbs Ethernet adapters. The improvement in writes is even greater with a 145% improvement in 256k write throughput and an 138% improvement in 1M write throughput. The two 100GbE Ethernet adapters are within 4% of the theoretical line rate of two 100GbE Ethernet adapters.

    This shows an increase in storage performance and means that it is beneficial for a SUSE Enterprise Linux environment to use 100GbE Ethernet adapters when using PowerFlex for storage. This benefit can be seen across the different test scenarios.

    This also indicates that the optimal network configuration for a SUSE Enterprise Linux environment using PowerFlex as the underlying storage platform is to leverage 100GbE Ethernet adapters instead of 25GbE Ethernet adapters.

Block volume testing - VMware 8.0.1 Testing

  • This section explores the testing results for a VMware ESXi host configured as a PowerFlex CO node using PowerFlex storage.

    Testing observations – VMware using the 25GBbE Ethernet adapter

    We began testing using the VMware virtual environment described in the System architecture section with the 25GbE Ethernet adapter. We used four network ports for the test. In PowerFlex, we mapped three 320GB volumes to the SDCs installed in four ESXi nodes, created, and mounted as datastores. We then created four SLES 15.4 VMs on the PowerFlex backed datastores.

    The VMware testing was conducted inside the SLES VMs, using the fio tool. The SUSE Linux Enterprise Server (SLES) VMs were then configured using the fio tool guidance. We then issued the fio command from a console to run a 20% random write test. The configuration of the fio command is detailed in Appendix B – fio configuration for all the test states.

    Evaluation of results for VMware ESXi volumes

    We compiled the results in the following charts to show the comparison of the 25GbE and 100GbE Ethernet adapters. The following charts compare the throughput results of four 25GbE Ethernet adapters, two 100GbE Ethernet adapters, and four 100GbE Ethernet adapters.

    Figure 14.    ESXi 8.0.1 – Read Throughput Comparison – Four 25GbE vs. Two 100GbE vs. Four 100GbE Ethernet adapters

    Figure 15.    ESXi 8.0.1 – Write Throughput Comparison – Four 25GbE vs. Two 100GbE vs. Four 100GbE Ethernet adapters

    The test results show that two 100GbE Ethernet adapters provide an almost 100% improvement in both 256k read throughput and 512k read throughput compared to four 25GbE Ethernet adapters. For write performance, two 100GbE Ethernet adapters provide a 67% improvement in 256k write throughput and an 80% improvement in 512k write throughput.

    This shows an increase in storage performance and means that it is beneficial for VMware ESXi environments to use 100GbE Ethernet adapters with PowerFlex storage. This benefit can be seen across the five different test scenarios in this section.

    This also indicates that the optimal network configuration for a SUSE Enterprise Linux environment using PowerFlex as the underlying storage platform is to leverage 100GbE Ethernet adapters to obtain increased storage throughput when compared with 25GbE Ethernet adapters.

Broadcom BCM57508 2x100GbE Ethernet Controllers – Overview

  • Based on Broadcom’s scalable 10/25/50/100/200G Ethernet controller architecture, the NetXtreme-E Series BCM57508 200G PCIe 4.0 Ethernet controller is designed to build highly scalable, feature-rich networking solutions in servers for enterprise and cloud-scale networking and storage applications, including high-performance computing, telco, machine learning, storage disaggregation, and data analytics.

    The BCM57508 200G PCIe 4.0 Ethernet Controller builds upon the success of the widely deployed NetXtreme E-Series architecture by combining a high-bandwidth Ethernet controller with a unique set of highly optimized hardware acceleration engines to enhance network performance and improve server efficiency.

    Driven by the growing need for higher server bandwidth and storage capacity to support new and emerging applications, enterprises, telcos and cloud providers are modernizing their data centers by adopting latest networking technologies, such as server virtualization and NVMe-oF. The resulting expansion in data volumes increases server-to-server traffic and CPU loads for networking tasks.

    With its market-leading hardware acceleration technologies, the NetXtreme-E Series BCM57508 200G PCIe 4.0 Ethernet Controller addresses performance and service demands of mega-scale data center networks with high throughput and advanced flow processing. Features such as TruFlow increase VM density up to 50 percent, freeing more CPU cycles for additional virtual machines. On-chip tunneling protocol processing for Geneve, VXLAN, and NVGRE provides up to a 5X throughput increase while lowering CPU utilization up to 90 percent compared to software-only solutions. NetXtreme-E Series solutions also support advanced networking technologies such as RoCE, SDN, and NFV, to facilitate the management of data networks and to enable service provider solutions.

    Figure 44.    BCM957508-P2100G Network Interface Card

    Building upon the success of the widely deployed Broadcom NetXtreme-E architecture, the BCM57500 series Ethernet Controllers set the bar higher by supporting single, dual, and quad-port configurations with 200 Gb/s aggregate throughput. The BCM57500 supports network interfaces of 200GbE, 100GbE, 50GbE, 40GbE, 25GbE, and 10GbE.

    Incorporating industry-leading PHY technology, the BCM57500 provides highly efficient network connectivity using eight lanes of built-in SerDes, each supporting 50G PAM-4 and 25G NRZ. When paired with Broadcom’s market-leading Ethernet switches StrataXGS or StrataDNS, the BCM57500 assures the highest level of performance, interoperability, and features.

    The BCM57500 supports RDMA over Converged Ethernet (RoCE) with hardware-based congestion control. Broadcom’s RoCE congestion control not only delivers the lowest latency in real-life scenarios but dramatically reduces the complexity of RoCE deployment at scale.

    The BCM57500 TruFlow technology integrates hardware acceleration with enhanced programmable parser/lookup/match/action engine. TruFlow increases virtual machine density and improves application performance.

    The BCM57500 TruTrust technology enables the industry’s most secure server platform with Broadcom’s Silicon Root of Trust and Secure Boot Loader. TruTrust provides absolute protection by locking down the lowest level resources against attacks.

    The BCM57500 is PCIe 4.0 compliant and backwards compatible with versions 3.0, 2.0, and 1.1.

    In this paper, we chose to use the 2-port 100GB configuration of the BCM57508 Ethernet controller. We did not test the 10/25/50/200G controller configurations.

Conclusion

  • The extensive testing performed clearly shows the performance advantages of using Broadcom 100GbE network interfaces in Dell PowerFlex software-defined infrastructure. Using 100GbE networking interfaces enhances PowerFlex’s unmatched performance, scalability, and workload consolidation. By adopting 100GbE networking in PowerFlex, customers can consolidate even more performance intensive applications.

    From this testing it is clear that the use of 100GbE networking is preferred over 25GbE to obtain the best performance from a PowerFlex environment. To discover more about optimal networking for PowerFlex storage, contact your Dell representative.

Dell PowerFlex overview

  • PowerFlex family

    PowerFlex software-defined infrastructure enables broad consolidation across the data center, encompassing almost any type of workload and architecture. The software-defined architecture offers automation and programmability of the complete infrastructure and provides scalability, performance, and resiliency to enable effortless adherence to stringent workload service level agreements (SLAs).

    The PowerFlex family provides a foundation that combines compute and high-performance storage resources in a managed unified fabric. PowerFlex comes in flexible deployment options (rack, appliance, or custom nodes and in the public cloud) that enable independent (two-layer), HCI (single-layer), or mixed architectures. PowerFlex is ideal for high-performance applications and databases, building an agile private/hybrid cloud, or consolidating resources in heterogeneous environments.

    Figure 40.    PowerFlex family

    PowerFlex software components

    Software is the key differentiation in the PowerFlex offering. PowerFlex software components not only provide software-defined storage services, but also help simplify infrastructure management and orchestration. This enables comprehensive IT Operational Management (ITOM) and Life Cycle Management (LCM) capabilities that span compute as well as storage infrastructure, from BIOS and firmware to nodes, software, and networking. 

    PowerFlex

    PowerFlex is the software foundation of PowerFlex software-defined infrastructure. It is a scale-out block and file storage service that is designed to deliver flexibility, elasticity, and simplicity with predictable high performance and resiliency at scale.

    PowerFlex Manager

    PowerFlex Manager is the software component in the PowerFlex family that enables ITOM automation and LCM capabilities for PowerFlex systems. Starting with PowerFlex 4.0, the unified PowerFlex Manager brings together three separate components that are used in previous releases, PowerFlex Manager, the core PowerFlex UI, and the PowerFlex gateway. The new PowerFlex UI runs in Kubernetes and embraces a modern development framework.

    PowerFlex with NVMe over TCP (NVMe/TCP)

    NVMe is a family of open specifications that defines an industry standard for both a logical interface and a communication protocol for accessing block storage across an internal PCIe fabric or through external fabrics such as TCP/IP and FC. NVMe is designed to take advantage of the internal parallelism and low latency inherent in flash-based media SSDs.

    NVMe/TCP is an extension of the NVMe base specification that defines the binding of the NVMe protocol to message-based fabrics using TCP. By binding the NVMe protocol to TCP, NVMe/TCP enables the efficient end-to-end transfer of commands and data between NVMe hosts and NVMe controller devices by any standard Ethernet-based TCP/IP networks.

    Figure 41.    PowerFlex with NVMe/TCP

    From PowerFlex version 4.x onwards, support for NVMe/TCP has been added for on-premises deployment with the introduction of a new Storage Data Target (SDT) component installed in the storage layer. The NVMe initiator in the OS or hypervisor communicates with the SDT, which then communicates with the Storage Data Server (SDS). The NVMe initiator is part of the kernel of the application host operating system or hypervisor.

    For more information, see PowerFlex with NVMe over TCP.

    PowerFlex deployment architectures 

    PowerFlex software-defined infrastructure excels in deployment flexibility. PowerFlex can be deployed in a two-layer (independent compute and storage layers), single-layer (hyperconverged infrastructure, or HCI), or a mixture of the two architectures (mixed). 

    Figure 42. PowerFlex deployment architectures

    Independent architecture

    In an independent architecture or two-layer architecture, some nodes provide storage capacity for data in applications, while other separate and independent nodes provide compute resources for applications and workloads. Compute and storage resources can be scaled independently by adding nodes to the cluster while it remains active. This separation of compute and storage resources helps to minimize software licensing costs in certain situations. This architecture can be ideal for high-performance databases and application workloads.

    Hyperconverged architecture

    In an HCI architecture, each node in the cluster contributes storage and compute resources simultaneously to the applications and workloads. This architecture allows you to scale your infrastructure uniformly with building blocks that add both storage and compute resources. This architecture is appropriate for data center and workload consolidation.

    Mixed architecture

    A mixed architecture is a combination of both the HCI and independent architectures. As shown in Figure 42. PowerFlex deployment architectures. There are some storage only nodes, compute only nodes, and HCI nodes as a part of the same PowerFlex cluster. This is a desirable architecture when working with an existing compute infrastructure and adding high-performance software-defined infrastructure. This can also be a starting point for a two-layer deployment design as external workloads are migrated to PowerFlex.

    PowerFlex consumption options

    PowerFlex rack

    PowerFlex rack is a software-defined infrastructure platform that delivers flexibility, elasticity, and simplicity with predictable performance and resiliency at scale by combining compute as well as high-performance storage resources in a managed unified network. This rack-based engineered system, with integrated networking, enables customers to achieve the scalability and management requirements of a modern data center.

    PowerFlex appliance

    PowerFlex appliance is a PowerEdge server which has been configured to be a node in a software-defined infrastructure deployment that runs PowerFlex software components. This offering allows customers the flexibility and savings to bring their own compatible networking.

    PowerFlex Custom Nodes

    PowerFlex Custom Nodes are validated server building-blocks configured for use with PowerFlex. They are available with thousands of configuration options and are available for customers who prefer to build their own environments.

    Dell APEX Block Storage for Public Cloud

    PowerFlex software is also available in the public cloud as Dell APEX Block Storage for Public Cloud. It offers the same on-premises benefits of high-performance, linear scalability, and high resilience as in cloud. It also adds cloud-specific benefits, such as large volume sizes, extreme performance based on NVMe drives, and predictable scalability. The Dell APEX Block Storage self-healing architecture simplifies and increases the availability of infrastructure. It is designed to remain running even when it encounters failures. With fast rebuilds, Dell APEX Block Storage recovers rapidly from failures and keeps operating, without degrading performance or compromising availability. You can also extend this availability and configure it to protect your application availability across multiple availability zones.

    PowerFlex CSI/CSM 

    An important component outside of PowerFlex that enables a flexible consumption model for Kubernetes is the PowerFlex CSI driver, developed as a part of the Dell Kubernetes strategy. After loading the CSI driver for PowerFlex into Kubernetes, it can be used to provision persistent volumes from the underlying PowerFlex storage resource. If the Kubernetes deployment is running low on PowerFlex storage resources, you can add PowerFlex storage nodes to increase the system capacity and performance. 

    The CSI driver connects the PowerFlex system and Kubernetes deployments. It is a storage broker which dynamically provisions volumes from PowerFlex through the PowerFlex API gateway to the Kubernetes cluster. Once the volume is available on PowerFlex, it is immediately mapped to the requesting pod. If a pod is destroyed or rescheduled, the CSI plug-in ensures that the volumes are remapped upon rescheduling of that pod. 

    Customers running Kubernetes clusters on PowerFlex use the Dell Container Storage Modules (CSM), which extend the CSI driver capabilities. These modules: 

    • Provide enterprise storage capabilities to Kubernetes for cloud-native stateful applications.
    • Reduce management complexity, so that developers can independently use enterprise storage with ease and automate daily operations.
    • Extend storage functionality and capabilities beyond using the CSI driver alone.

    These modules include snapshot, observability, authorization, application mobility, and resiliency. 

    PowerFlex supports multiple operating systems, different deployment options, and on-premises and public cloud deployment models (available in AWS and Azure). PowerFlex is validated with the leading Kubernetes distributions as shown in the following figure:

    Figure 43.    PowerFlex for different Kubernetes distributions

    Kubernetes containers

    Kubernetes is an open-source container orchestration system that is portable and can be extended to manage containerized workloads and services. Thus, Kubernetes facilitates both declarative configuration and automation. Containers are an effective way to bundle and run your applications because they each have their own file system, CPU, memory, process space, and more. As the containers are decoupled from the underlying infrastructure, they are portable across clouds and OS distributions. Kubernetes provides a framework to run distributed systems resiliently.

    For more information about Kubernetes, see the Kubernetes documentation.

    Dell CSM Modules

    Dell Technologies provides various CSM that are designed to help organizations manage their containerized applications efficiently. These modules provide persistent storage for containerized applications running in a cloud-native environment, while also addressing the challenges of storage in container environments, such as data persistence, scalability, and data protection.

    Dell CSM provide a range of features and capabilities that can help organizations manage their containerized applications efficiently, while ensuring scalability, flexibility, and data protection.

    The current features available with Dell CSM are:

    • Snapshots: Built on the CSIs point-in-time recovery with additional capabilities such as group and crash consistent snapshots with referential integrity. CSM for Volume Group Snapshots allows to take crash consistent snapshots of all the volumes that are attached to a pod simultaneously avoiding inconsistent or corrupt volumes which can be used for backup, testing, and restoring.
    • Authorization: CSM for Authorization provides storage and Kubernetes administrators the ability to apply Role-Based Access Control (RBAC) for Dell CSI Drivers.
    • Resiliency: CSM for Resiliency is designed to make Kubernetes applications, including the ones that use persistent storage, more resilient to various failures.
    • Application Mobility: CSM for Application Mobility provides Kubernetes administrators the ability to clone their stateful application workloads and application data to other clusters, either on-premises or in the cloud.
    • Replication: CSM for Replication is part of the open-source suite of Kubernetes storage enablers for Dell products.
    • Observability: CSM for Observability is part of the open-source suite of Kubernetes storage enablers for Dell products.
    • Encryption: Encryption provides the capability to encrypt user data residing on volumes created by Dell CSI Drivers.

    For more information, see Dell Container Storage Module.

fio CLI Command

  • The fio tool has many arguments that can be passed to it. In this section we describe the arguments used for testing in the environment as defined in the fio documentation. For more information about fio visit https://fio.readthedocs.io/en/latest/

    The following is the example fio command that was used to test the PowerFlex environment with Linux CO nodes.

    fio --name=$OUTPUTFILE --readwrite=randrw --rwmixwrite=$RWMIXWRITE --bs=$BLOCKSIZE --invalidate=1 --direct=1 --group_reporting --filename=/dev/scinia --filename=/dev/scinib --filename=/dev/scinic --time_based --runtime=100 --refill_buffers --norandommap --randrepeat=0 --ioengine=libaio --numjobs=$NUMJOBS --iodepth=$QUEUEDEPTH --output-format=json --output=/root/$OUTPUTFILE.json

    This command performs the following actions:

    • --name=<str>
      ASCII name of the job. This may be used to override the name printed by fio for this job. Otherwise, the job name is used. On the command line this parameter has the special purpose of also signaling the start of a new job.
      Using variable: $OUTPUTFILE
    • --readwrite=randrw
      Instructs fio to run in a random read/write configuration
    • --rwmixwrite=<int write percentage>
      Percentage of a mixed workload that should be writes.
      Using variable: $RWMIXWRITE
    • --bs=<Block size in KiB ([int]k)>
      Block size used in KiB
      Using variable: $BLOCKSIZE
    • --invalidate=1
      Invalidate the buffer/page cache parts of the files to be used prior to starting I/O if the platform and file type support it. Defaults to true. This will be ignored if pre_read is also specified for the same job.
    • --direct=1
      If value is true, use non-buffered I/O. This is usually O_DIRECT. Note that OpenBSD and ZFS on Solaris don’t support direct I/O. On Windows the synchronous ioengines don’t support direct I/O. Default: false.
    • --group_reporting
      To see the final report per-group instead of per-job, use group_reporting. Jobs in a file will be part of the same reporting group, unless if separated by a stonewall, or by using new_group.
    • --filename=<device name>
      fio normally creates a filename based on the job name, thread number, and file number (see filename_format). If you want to share files between threads in a job or several jobs with fixed file paths, specify a filename for each of them to override the default. If the I/O engine is file based, you can specify a number of files by separating the names with a ‘:’ colon. If you want a job to open /dev/sda and /dev/sdb as the two working files, you can use filename=/dev/sda:/dev/sdb. This also means that whenever this option is specified, nrfiles is ignored. The size of regular files specified by this option will be size divided by number of files unless an explicit size is specified by file size.
      Using variable: Based on OS mount paths.
    • --time_based
      If set, fio runs for the duration of the runtime specified even if the file(s) are completely read or written. It will simply loop over the same workload as many times as the runtime allows.
    • --runtime=100<seconds>
      Limit runtime. The test will run until it completes the configured I/O workload or until it has run for this specified amount of time, whichever occurs first. It can be difficult to determine for how long a specified job will run, so this parameter can cap the total runtime to a given time. When the unit is omitted, the value is interpreted in seconds.
    • --refill_buffers
      If this option is given, fio refills the I/O buffers on every submit.
    • --norandommap
      Normally fio will cover every block of the file when doing random I/O. If this option is given, fio will just get a new random offset without looking at past I/O history. This means that some blocks may not be read or written, and that some blocks may be read/written more than once. If this option is used with verify and multiple blocksizes (using bsrange), only intact blocks are verified, and partially overwritten blocks are ignored. With an async I/O engine and an I/O depth > 1, it is possible for the same block to be overwritten, which can cause verification errors. Either do not use norandommap in this case, or also use the lfsr random generator.
    • --randrepeat=0
      Seed all random number generators in a predictable way so the pattern is repeatable across runs. Default: true.
    • --ioengine=libaio
      Defines how the job issues I/O to the file. Libaio is Linux native asynchronous I/O. Note that Linux may only support queued behavior with non-buffered I/O (set direct=1 or buffered=0). This engine defines engine specific options.
    • --numjobs=<int>
      Create the specified number of clones of this job. Each clone of job is spawned as an independent thread or process. May be used to setup a larger number of threads/processes doing the same thing. Each thread is reported separately; to see statistics for all clones as a whole, use group_reporting in conjunction with new_group. See --max-jobs. Default: 1.
      Using variable: $NUMJOBS
    • --iodepth=<queue depth>
      Number of I/O units to keep in flight against the file. Note that increasing iodepth beyond 1 will not affect synchronous I/O engines (except for small degrees when verify_async is in use). Even async engines may impose OS restrictions causing the desired depth not to be achieved. This may happen on Linux when using libaio and not setting direct=1, since buffered I/O is not async on that OS. Check the I/O depth distribution in the fio output to verify that the achieved depth is as expected. Default: 1.
      Using variable: $QUEUEDEPTH
    • --output-format=json
      Set the reporting format to normal, terse, json, or json+. Multiple formats can be selected, separated by a comma. terse is a CSV based format. json+ is like JSON but adds a full dump of the latency buckets.
    • --output=/root/$OUTPUTFILE.json
      Write output to file filename.
      Using variable: $OUTPUTFILE

Hypothesis

  • We wanted to test the difference between 25GbE and 100GbE Ethernet adapters to observe what impacts it had on throughput and where network bottlenecks were located. In the test configurations used, we wanted to examine if it was possible to fully saturate the network links in the various configurations. The expectation being that by using to 100GbE Ethernet adapters there would be more than sufficient bandwidth to support the demands of the tested operating systems.

Network architecture


  • Beyond the Ethernet controllers the network infrastructure (including switches and cables) plays an important role in the performance of any storage environment. In this section we look at the PowerFlex networking architecture and its configuration.

    Physical network architecture

    The physical network for the test environment is composed of two Dell S5232F-ON 100GbE top of rack (TOR) switches and a separate management switch dedicated to management traffic, including iDRAC connectivity.

    When testing the BCM57508 Ethernet 100GbE adapters we used 100GbE QSFP28 cables. For testing of the BMC57414 Ethernet adapters we used QSFP breakout cables connected to the Dell S5232F-ON switches. This reduced change to the test environment between tests and ensured switch consistency across tests.

    Logical network architecture

    The logical network architecture is shown in the following diagram.

    Figure 3.   Logical network architecture

    At the physical layer, two supported TOR switches are used for redundancy and load-balancing purposes. All network ports are configured as trunks carrying the necessary VLANs. VLANs are created to separate different network traffic. No QoS settings were configured for the different VLANs.

    VLAN configuration

    PowerFlex uses several different VLANs for communication and traffic isolation. The following table shows the different VLAN networks that were configured for the testing environment:

    Table 5.      VLANs configuration

    Network Type

    VLAN ID

    Ingress/API/OS Management

    105

    PowerFlex Management

    150

    PowerFlex Data 1

    151

    PowerFlex Data 2

    152

    Virtual networking for the VMware ESXi Host

    For the VMware virtual environment, additional virtual network configuration was necessary. We used a VMware vSwitch. The trunked network connections for the PowerFlex Data were added to the standard vSwitch and the VLANs were configured accordingly as port groups on the standard vSwitch. The standard vSwitch was configured with an MTU of 9000 to support jumbo frames.

Overview

  • Modern infrastructures can benefit from advances in network speed. In this white paper we examine the benefits of using Broadcom BCM57508 Ethernet controllers as part of a Dell PowerFlex environment. Specifically, we explore the impact they make to the storage environment and how performance increases substantially when using Broadcom 100GbE network interface cards (NICs).

    We start by providing an overview of the technology used in our design. We then look at the test results and explore how an organization can benefit from leveraging PowerFlex with 100GbE networking to obtain a significant boost in the overall performance of their environment.

    The performance increase from the Broadcom NICs means that PowerFlex can deliver a substantial boost to the whole PowerFlex environment. This translates into increased throughput with fewer nodes required to achieve the same storage speeds which could potentially reduce the required storage footprint for organizations, depending on throughput and capacity requirements.

PowerFlex testing architecture

  • For the performance characterization we used a two-tier PowerFlex (v4.5.1.103) architecture with a medium granularity (MG) data layout. There is no discernible difference in the performance of the MG data layout compared with fine granularity (FG) versions, and the performance characteristics observed in this paper should be consistent with other versions of PowerFlex in both the 3.6 and 4.x series.

    The architecture used in this white paper is not designed to validate the platforms that run on PowerFlex, or to validate a set of best practices. Our intention is to operate the system at its limit and control the variables that can impede that storage performance, thereby demonstrating the capabilities of an individual component.

    Actual results for workloads may vary from the testing in this paper, and it is important that organizational outcomes are considered and applied as necessary to obtain both the correct level of performance and capabilities needed.

    Our testing consisted of both virtualized and bare-metal environments to align with commonly deployed operating systems and hypervisors.

    VMware by Broadcom virtual environment

    The environment consisted of either one or four compute only (CO) nodes with VMware ESXi installed and four PowerFlex storage-only (SO) nodes. The VMware ESXi host was configured with build 8.0.1 – 21495797. The vCenter used to manage the environment was deployed in a separate management cluster so as not to impact testing.

    All testing virtual machines (VMs) were installed on local storage to avoid impacting test performance. Under normal operating conditions, it is not advisable to run production workloads on local storage due to its associated limitations, for example VMware High Availability (HA) events.

    Each CO node had the PowerFlex Storage Data Client (SDC) software installed and a single VM for testing. The testing VM was a SUSE Linux VM with the following configuration:

Test methodology

  • Flexible IO tester

    Flexible I/O tester (fio) (https://fio.readthedocs.io/) is an open-source, benchmarking tool, capable of simulating block device I/O patterns observed in real-world applications. For all tests conducted inside of VMs or on bare-metal nodes, fio versions 3.35 and 3.36 were used.

    Test deployment

    The PowerFlex SDC and fio tester were installed on both the Linux CO nodes and VMware ESXi CO nodes. For bare-metal testing, specified workloads were executed on raw PowerFlex volumes provisioned to the Linux CO nodes without file systems. Additionally, for VMware ESXi testing, the fio tester was installed in a Linux VM located on datastores backed by PowerFlex volumes

    The full test suite was run using four 25GbE Ethernet adapters followed by two – 100GbE Ethernet adapters. For more details on how the fio command was configured for these tests refer to Appendix B – fio configuration.

Variable values for fio

  • The variables used in the fio command were given the following values during testing:

    RWMIXWRITE = [0, 20, 50, 80, 100]

    BLOCKSIZE = [512b, 4k, 8k, 16k, 32k, 64k, 128k, 256k, 512k, 1m]

    NUMJOBS = [1, 4, 8, 16, 24, 32]

    QUEUEDEPTH = [1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128, 256]

    NUMJOBS*QUEUEDEPTH <=1024
